7th–8th Grade PE · Unit 1.1 · Intro to Physical Education (P.E.)
Week 1

Welcome, Junior Exercise Physiologist

Movement used to be something you just did. This year you take a more serious lens. As a junior exercise physiologist, your job is to design protocols, measure baselines, run interventions, and analyze whether the evidence actually supports what coaches and influencers say. By the end of the year you should be able to read a training plan, spot the missing variable, and propose a study that would settle the argument.

1
Lesson 1
What an Exercise Physiologist Actually Does

Exercise physiology is the science of how the body responds to physical stress — short-term during a workout, and long-term across weeks and years of training. Researchers in this field run controlled experiments: they measure a baseline, deliver a precise intervention (a workout, a supplement, a sleep schedule), then re-measure to see what changed. The goal is not opinion. The goal is evidence.

That same scientific lens is what separates a coach who guesses from one who knows. When a trainer says "this drill builds explosiveness," a junior physiologist asks: How would we know? What would we measure? Compared to what control? Over how many weeks? Those four questions are the foundation of every training decision you'll learn to make this year.

🧪Sport Science

The current evidence-based recommendation for kids 6–17 is at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity daily, plus muscle- and bone-strengthening activity on three days per week. That number comes from large studies tracking thousands of children for decades. But notice the precision: not "be active," but 60 minutes, moderate-to-vigorous, daily, with strength work 3×/week. That's the kind of dose-specific recommendation a physiologist looks for.

2
Lesson 2
The Five Systems Under the Hood

An exercise physiologist treats the body as a network of interlocking systems, each adapting to training stress on its own timeline. The systems share work, but they don't share recovery rates — one of the most important things to understand about your own body.

❤️
Cardiovascular
Heart, blood, vessels. Adapts within 4–6 weeks of consistent aerobic work.
🫁
Respiratory
Lungs and breathing muscles. Adapts fastest — measurable changes in 2–3 weeks.
💪
Muscular
Roughly 600 muscles. Strength gains in 6–8 weeks; size changes in 8–12.
🦴
Skeletal
206 bones. Adapt slowly — bone density changes take 6+ months of loading.
🧠
Nervous
Brain and nerves. Coordination improvements show in days. Neural strength gains: 2–4 weeks.
💡Did You Know?

The first measurable adaptation to a new training program is almost always neural, not muscular. In the first 2–4 weeks, you get stronger mostly because your nervous system learns to recruit more muscle fibers at once — not because the fibers themselves grow. Visible muscle growth (hypertrophy) takes 8–12 weeks of consistent training. Knowing this protects you from giving up after a month of "no visible change."

3
Lesson 3
Why the Brain Is Part of the Training

Every workout you do also changes your brain. Exercise releases endorphins and elevates BDNF — brain-derived neurotrophic factor — a protein that helps neurons grow and connect. Studies on adolescents show that students who exercise regularly score better on attention, memory, and executive-function tests than matched peers who don't.

But the evidence is not unlimited. The effect on academic grades is real but modest — roughly a 0.1–0.3 grade-point bump on average. The effect on mood is larger and more consistent. The effect on sleep quality is also robust. A junior physiologist treats movement as one input among many — important, but not magic.

📊Case Study

The "Hancock Park" attention study (multiple replications, 2014–2022): Researchers measured 6th–8th graders' performance on a sustained-attention task before and after 20 minutes of moderate exercise. Across more than a dozen studies, exercise produced an average 4–7% improvement in attention scores that lasted up to two hours. The effect was bigger in kids with lower baseline fitness. Lesson: a movement break before a hard mental task is supported by real evidence — but it doesn't replace sleep, hydration, or actually studying.

4
Lesson 4
The Skills That Don't Show on a Stopwatch

Performance is more than physical output. Sports researchers measure a parallel set of skills they call psychological readiness — communication, leadership, emotional regulation, persistence after failure. These are harder to test but predict long-term success in sport as strongly as physical metrics do, sometimes more.

The clearest example is grit research: studies tracking athletes across multiple seasons find that the ability to keep training through plateaus is a better predictor of who reaches the highest level than initial talent. Talent gets you noticed; consistency gets you somewhere.

🌎Real-World Connection

Most professional teams now employ performance psychologists alongside strength coaches and athletic trainers. The NBA, NFL, and most MLB teams have mental-performance specialists on staff. Olympic teams have done this since the 1980s. The job is not therapy — it's training arousal regulation, visualization, focus skills, and recovery from setbacks. Career paths include sport psychology, exercise physiology, athletic training, biomechanics, and nutrition science — all of them growing fields.

🔬Coach's Lab

4-week protocol: build your baseline portfolio. An exercise physiologist starts every program with measurements. This week, record four baselines: (1) resting heart rate, taken first thing in the morning for three consecutive days, then averaged; (2) max push-ups in 60 seconds, with good form; (3) max plank hold in seconds; (4) how many minutes you can jog without stopping. Save these numbers. Re-test all four in Week 4. Save the new numbers. We'll do this every month all year — that's how you build evidence of your own adaptations instead of guessing.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Exercise physiology — The science of how the body responds to short-term and long-term physical stress.
  • Baseline — A starting measurement used to evaluate change after an intervention.
  • Intervention — A planned change introduced to test an effect — a workout, diet, or sleep schedule.
  • Resting heart rate — Beats per minute at full rest. Generally drops with cardiovascular training.
  • BDNF — Brain-derived neurotrophic factor — a protein released by exercise that helps neurons grow (stretch term).
  • Hypertrophy — Increase in muscle fiber size; takes 8–12 weeks of consistent training to become visible (stretch term).
  • Psychological readiness — Mental and emotional state required for peak performance (stretch term).
  • Effect size — How big a measured difference is — distinct from whether it exists at all (stretch term).
📝Weekly Reflection

Critique prompt: An online influencer claims that a single 20-minute morning workout will "transform your focus and grades for the day." Based on what you read above, name three reasons their claim is partly supported AND three reasons it's overstated. What additional information would you want before recommending this to a friend who is struggling in school?

→What's Next

Next: launch your first VR Fitness Park assignment, then kick off Flight Club with a movement challenge that tests your new baseline data.

Flight Club

Flight Club Guidelines

Welcome to Flight Club — the lab where you take everything you've studied and test it on your own body. Every other week, a new movement challenge drops. You complete it, record the data, and earn Flight Club credit. Here's how the system works.

1
Mission
What Flight Club Is

Flight Club is the active research arm of Mission: Move! Each module ends with a Flight Club challenge — a short, focused movement task connected to that module's topic. It's where lesson content becomes experimental data.

Some challenges target strength. Some target endurance. Some test coordination, energy systems, or sportsmanship under fatigue. They're engineered to take 5–15 minutes and require minimal equipment.

2
Rules
Flight Club Rules
  1. Read the full challenge first. Know what you're doing before you start.
  2. Warm up. 2–3 minutes of light cardio plus dynamic stretches.
  3. Follow the steps in order. Don't skip — order matters.
  4. Modify, don't quit. Too hard? Reduce reps or scale down. Too easy? Add reps or shorten rest.
  5. Cool down. 2–3 minutes of slow movement plus static stretches.
  6. Hydrate — water before, during, and after.
  7. Submit your proof. Photo, video, or written reflection — whatever the challenge asks.
3
Crew
What Is the Flight Crew Check-In?

At the end of every challenge you'll find a Flight Crew Check-In — two short reflection questions. They aren't optional. An exercise physiologist trains their thinking as much as their body. The Check-In asks you to notice what you did, identify which energy system or fitness component was at work, and decide what you'd change next time. For 7/8 grade, expect questions that push toward dose-response thinking: would doubling the volume double the gain, or would you hit diminishing returns? At what point would more start hurting instead of helping?

Detailed, data-rich reflections earn extra Flight Club credit.

4
Safety
Safety First, Always
  • Check your space — clear of clutter, enough room to move
  • Wear safe shoes (closed-toe with grip)
  • Stop if something hurts beyond normal training discomfort
  • Ask a trusted adult if you're unsure about a move
  • Follow the 10% rule — don't increase your weekly Flight Club volume by more than 10%
💡Did You Know?

Elite athletes call recovery and self-review "the secret 1%." They spend roughly 80% of training time on training, 19% on competition — and that final 1% on reviewing what worked and what didn't. It's the smallest slice, but sport scientists who study elite performance consistently identify it as one of the strongest predictors of long-term improvement. The Flight Crew Check-In is your 1%.

→What's Next

Ready? Your first Flight Club starts in Module 1.1, Week 2. Bring your A-game.

7th–8th Grade PE · Unit 1.2 · Warm-Ups and Cool Downs
Week 3

Warm-Ups and Cool-Downs: Engineering the Transition

Most athletes treat warm-ups as a ritual — something to do before the real work. An exercise physiologist treats the warm-up as the first intervention of the session: a measurable shift in core temperature, blood flow, neural readiness, and hormonal state. The cool-down is the same intervention running in reverse, pulling the body back toward homeostasis so that recovery can start. Skip either one and there's a measurable performance cost. Get them right and the data shows in your numbers.

1
Lesson 1
The Physiology of the Warm-Up

A warm-up is a 5–15 minute sequence of progressive low-intensity movement that shifts the body from rest to performance state. During it, core body temperature rises 1–2°C, heart rate climbs gradually, joints release synovial fluid (a lubricant), and nerve-to-muscle signaling becomes faster and more precise. Each one of these changes is measurable. Each one improves performance.

The standard structure has three phases. (1) General warm-up: 3–5 minutes of light cardio to raise heart rate and temperature. (2) Dynamic mobility: 4–6 minutes of controlled, sport-specific movement through full range. (3) Neural priming: 2–3 minutes of short bursts at near-game intensity to "wake up" the nervous system. A high jumper might end with three near-max jumps; a basketball player with a few hard sprints. Then you go.

🧪Sport Science

Dynamic stretching (moving through range) and static stretching (holding a position) produce opposite results when used before a power activity. A 2014 meta-analysis of more than 100 studies found that static stretches held over 60 seconds reduce subsequent jump height and sprint speed by 2–5%. Short static holds (under 30 seconds) have a much smaller effect. The professional consensus: dynamic before performance; static after, or in separate flexibility sessions.

2
Lesson 2
Cool-Downs and the Parasympathetic Switch

A cool-down is a 5–10 minute period of slowing movement and slow breathing that drops the body out of high-arousal sympathetic mode into parasympathetic (rest-and-recover) mode. The cardiovascular system benefits from the gradual taper — without it, blood can pool in your legs (your muscle pumps stop helping it return) and cause dizziness. The nervous system benefits even more: deep breathing during cool-down has been shown to lower heart rate variability stress markers within minutes.

A complete cool-down has three components: 2–3 minutes of light movement (walking or easy jog), 5–8 static stretches of 20–30 seconds each focused on the muscles you trained, and a final 1–2 minutes of slow nasal breathing (in 4 seconds, out 6). That last piece is what flips the parasympathetic switch.

💡Did You Know?

For most of the 20th century, coaches blamed muscle soreness on lactic acid pooling in the muscles. We now know that's false. Lactate is a fuel your body recycles within hours. The next-day soreness called DOMS (delayed-onset muscle soreness) actually comes from microscopic damage in muscle fibers that triggers an inflammatory repair response. It peaks 24–72 hours after training. A cool-down doesn't prevent DOMS — but evidence does support that it speeds recovery from the cardiovascular and neural stress of the session.

3
Try It
Dynamic Warm-Up Sequence (6 minutes)
🔄
Arm Circles
30s — opens shoulders, primes rotator cuff stability.
🦵
High Knees
45s — raises core temperature, activates hip flexors.
↔️
Leg Swings
10 per leg forward + side — opens hip joint capsule, primes hamstrings and adductors.
🚶
Walking Lunges
10 steps — activates quads, glutes, and core stabilizers in one chain.
🌀
World's Greatest Stretch
5 per side — lunge + rotation. Hits hip flexors, T-spine, and shoulders.
⚡
A-Skips
20 yards — primes nervous system for sprinting mechanics.
4
Try It
Cool-Down Sequence (8 minutes)
🚶
Easy Walk
2 minutes — slows heart rate gradually.
🤲
Standing Toe Touch
30s — hamstrings and lower back release.
🦩
Quad Stretch
20s per side — quadriceps lengthening.
🦋
Butterfly Stretch
45s — opens hip adductors.
💪
Shoulder + Tricep
20s per side — upper body recovery.
🌬️
Box Breathing
8 cycles of 4-in / 4-hold / 6-out — engages parasympathetic recovery.
📊Case Study

FIFA 11+ injury-prevention program (2010 trial, 1,892 female soccer players): Researchers tested a structured 20-minute warm-up of running drills, strength, plyometrics, and balance. Teams that performed it twice weekly had 30–50% fewer injuries than control teams that did their normal warm-ups. The protocol is now used by youth soccer programs worldwide. Lesson: a well-designed warm-up isn't just performance prep — it's the cheapest injury-prevention tool in the gym.

🌎Real-World Connection

Every professional sports team employs athletic trainers whose entire job is designing warm-up and recovery protocols. An NBA pre-game warm-up can last 30 minutes and includes player-specific drills. Elite endurance athletes use heart-rate monitors to verify they've hit target zones before the gun goes off. NFL teams measure body temperature to confirm players have crossed the threshold where injury risk drops. The professionals take this seriously because the data shows it works.

🔬Coach's Lab

4-week protocol: prove the warm-up effect on yourself. Pick one measurable test — vertical jump, broad jump, or max push-ups in 30 seconds. Week 1: test cold (no warm-up) and record. Weeks 2–4: perform a full 6-minute dynamic warm-up before every workout, three sessions per week. Week 4: re-test cold AND after a full warm-up. You should see two changes: your warmed-up number should be 5–10% higher than your cold number, AND your cold number itself may improve from the training effect of three weeks of regular work. Track both. If the warm-up effect is large but the cold number didn't move, the gap tells you something about your nervous system's ability to recruit on demand.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Warm-up — A planned progressive sequence of low-intensity movement done before training.
  • Cool-down — A planned slow-down period after training to return the body to baseline.
  • Dynamic stretching — Controlled stretches done while moving — best before activity.
  • Static stretching — Holding a stretched position — best after activity or in flexibility sessions.
  • Range of motion (ROM) — How far a joint can move comfortably under control.
  • Parasympathetic — The nervous system mode responsible for rest, digestion, and recovery (stretch term).
  • Synovial fluid — Joint lubricant; warm-ups stimulate its release (stretch term).
  • DOMS — Delayed-onset muscle soreness — peaks 24–72 hours post-training (stretch term).
📝Weekly Reflection

Multi-variable design prompt: Design a sport-specific 8-minute warm-up for a sport you actually play. List every move, in order, with timing. For each move, identify which one of the four physiological goals it serves: (1) raise core temperature, (2) mobilize a joint, (3) activate a muscle group, or (4) prime the nervous system. Then justify why the order matters — what happens if you do neural priming first instead of last?

→What's Next

Next: build your own warm-up and cool-down routine in this week's VR assignment, then test it in Flight Club.

7th–8th Grade PE · Unit 1.3 · Muscular Strength and Endurance
Week 5

Muscular Strength and Endurance: Designing the Adaptation

Strength and endurance live close together in conversation but far apart in physiology. An exercise physiologist treats them as different abilities, built through different training stimuli, recovered on different timelines, and matched to different positions and sports. This week we map the difference, then dig into two ideas that govern almost every training plan ever written: the FITT principle for organizing variables, and progressive overload for forcing adaptation.

1
Lesson 1
Strength vs. Endurance: Two Different Abilities

Muscular strength is the maximum force a muscle can produce in a single effort. Muscular endurance is how long a muscle can keep producing force before fatigue. They're related but not the same number. A powerlifter has enormous strength and limited endurance. A marathon runner has enormous endurance and modest strength. Most field athletes need both — soccer players need to sustain 90 minutes of work and still win a tackle in the 89th minute.

The recipe to build each is different too. Heavy load + low reps + long rest = strength dominant. Lighter load + high reps + short rest = endurance dominant. Mix and match for hybrid sport demands.

2
Lesson 2
Major Muscle Groups Worth Knowing by Name
🦵
Quadriceps
Front of thigh. Knee extension — power for jumping and sprinting.
🦵
Hamstrings
Back of thigh. Knee flexion + hip extension. Critical for deceleration and top-end speed.
🍑
Glutes
Largest muscle group in the body. Primary driver of acceleration in sprinting.
🎯
Core
Abdominals, obliques, deep stabilizers. Transfers force between upper and lower body.
💪
Biceps + Triceps
Elbow flexion + extension. Used in pulling and pushing actions.
🪶
Latissimus Dorsi
"Lats" — wide back muscles powering pull-ups, climbing, and swim strokes.
🧪Sport Science

Training creates microscopic damage to muscle fibers. During recovery — mostly during deep sleep — your body repairs the fibers and adds extra protein, making them slightly larger and stronger. This process is called muscle protein synthesis (MPS), and it peaks in the 24–48 hours after a hard workout. Eating 0.25–0.4 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight within an hour of training amplifies the response. For a 50 kg athlete, that's roughly 15–20 grams — about a cup of milk or a small chicken breast. Rest days aren't optional; they're when the building happens.

3
Lesson 3
FITT and Progressive Overload

Every coach's training plan organizes around four variables, captured in the acronym FITT:

  • Frequency — sessions per week
  • Intensity — how hard each session is (weight, speed, effort)
  • Time — duration, sets, reps
  • Type — modality (resistance, cardio, plyometric, sport-specific)

Change any one of these and you change the training stress. The single most important principle on top of FITT is progressive overload: to keep getting stronger, you must gradually increase the demand. The body adapts to the exact load it sees and then stops adapting. To keep progressing, you bump one variable — add a rep, add a set, add resistance, or shorten rest. Most plans bump just one variable per week. Bumping all four at once usually leads to injury or overtraining.

The companion concept is the recovery-to-stress ratio. Adaptation happens only when stress is followed by sufficient recovery. Too much stress, too little recovery = overtraining. Too little stress, plenty of recovery = no progress. The art of a good training plan is calibrating both sides.

💡Did You Know?

The strongest muscle in the body — relative to its size — is the masseter, the jaw closer. It can generate up to 200 pounds of force on your back teeth. But the largest and most powerful muscle group is the gluteus maximus. Studies of elite sprinters show that glute size and activation are among the best predictors of acceleration in the first 10 meters of a sprint. This is why nearly every modern speed-development program features hip thrusts and Romanian deadlifts at its core.

4
Try It
Bodyweight Strength Circuit

You don't need a weight room to train strength. Your body is a complete resistance system. Try this circuit, then apply progressive overload over the next 3 weeks — add 1–2 reps per exercise per week, or shorten rest between sets by 10 seconds. Track the numbers.

🦾
Push-Ups
10–15 reps. Chest, shoulders, triceps, core.
🏋️
Bodyweight Squats
15–20 reps. Quads, glutes, hamstrings as one chain.
📏
Plank Hold
30–60 seconds. Core endurance in isometric load.
🌉
Glute Bridges
12–15 reps. Glutes and posterior chain.
🚶
Reverse Lunges
10 per leg. Single-leg strength + balance.
🪜
Inverted Rows
8–12 reps under a table. Pulls — often missing from home workouts.
📊Case Study

Eliud Kipchoge's strength program (Vienna, 2019 sub-2-hour marathon): Kipchoge runs 130–200 km per week, but he also lifts heavy two days per week — squats, lunges, core work. Why would a marathon runner train strength? Because strength training improves running economy (the energy cost per stride) by roughly 4–8% even in elite endurance athletes, according to multiple controlled studies. That's the difference between a 2:01 marathon and the historic 1:59:40 he ran. Lesson: strength is not optional even in pure endurance sports.

🌎Real-World Connection

Strength training pays off far past sport. Firefighters need it to climb stairs in 80 pounds of gear. Nurses need it to lift patients safely. Construction workers need it to swing tools for 8 hours. Even office workers train strength to protect their backs from a lifetime of sitting. Bone density built before age 20 sets your ceiling for adult bone health — a system that becomes critical 50 years later when osteoporosis risk rises. The strength foundation you lay now is part of a body you'll carry the rest of your life.

🔬Coach's Lab

4-week strength protocol with built-in evaluation. Week 1: Test max push-ups in 60 seconds with good form. Record the number. Train push-ups three sessions this week (3 sets of 8–10, every other day). Week 2: Add one rep per set (3 sets of 9–11). Week 3: Add another rep AND shorten rest by 15 seconds. Week 4: Re-test max push-ups in 60 seconds. Calculate percent change: (new − old) / old × 100. A 10–20% gain in 4 weeks is realistic. If your number didn't move, examine the variables: did you actually train 3 sessions per week, or skip one? Did you sleep enough? Was your form the same in both tests? A real physiologist diagnoses by looking at the data — not by guessing.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Muscular strength — Maximum force a muscle can produce in a single effort.
  • Muscular endurance — How long a muscle can produce force before fatiguing.
  • Rep / repetition — One complete cycle of an exercise.
  • Set — A group of reps performed without rest.
  • FITT principle — Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type — the four training variables (stretch term).
  • Progressive overload — Gradually increasing training demand to keep forcing adaptation (stretch term).
  • Muscle protein synthesis (MPS) — The repair-and-rebuild process that makes muscles stronger after training (stretch term).
  • Recovery-to-stress ratio — The balance between training load and recovery time; both sides matter (stretch term).
📝Weekly Reflection

Multi-variable design prompt: Using FITT, design a 3-week strength program for a sport you play. Specify F, I, T, T for each week. Then explain how you'll apply progressive overload — which variable will you bump in Week 2 vs. Week 3, and why that one? Finally, identify the recovery-to-stress ratio you're targeting (how many rest days per week, why that many for your sport).

→What's Next

Next: design and run your own strength protocol in Week 6, then test it in Flight Club.

7th–8th Grade PE · Unit 1.4 · Cardiovascular Fitness
Week 7

Cardiovascular Fitness: Training the Engine Across Three Energy Systems

Cardiovascular fitness is the single strongest predictor of long-term health that researchers have ever measured. Across more than 50 years of large prospective studies, low cardiorespiratory fitness predicts mortality more powerfully than smoking, high cholesterol, or obesity. The good news is that the system is highly trainable, especially in adolescence. This week we'll go beyond "do cardio" into the three energy systems that fuel different sports, the heart-rate zones used to target each one, and the modern metric (HRV) that elite athletes use to dose their training.

1
Lesson 1
Inside the Cardiovascular System

The cardiovascular system is a closed loop with three pieces: the heart (a fist-sized muscle pumping roughly 100,000 times a day), blood vessels (arteries, veins, and capillaries that form the highway), and blood (carrying oxygen out and waste back). Train the system and every component improves — heart walls thicken slightly, blood volume increases, capillary density in muscles grows.

The headline metric is VO₂ max — the maximum volume of oxygen your body can use during all-out exercise, measured in milliliters per kilogram per minute. Untrained adults score around 35–40 ml/kg/min. Elite endurance athletes routinely measure above 70. Tour de France winners have hit 85+. VO₂ max is roughly 50% genetic and 50% trainable. The biggest gains happen in adolescence — what you build at your age sets the ceiling you'll defend for decades.

2
Lesson 2
The Three Energy Systems

Your muscles burn a chemical called ATP (adenosine triphosphate), but the body produces it through three different pathways. Each dominates at a different effort and duration:

⚡
ATP-PC System
All-out efforts under 10 seconds. Powers sprints, jumps, single heavy lifts. No oxygen required.
🔥
Glycolytic System
Hard efforts from 10 seconds to roughly 2 minutes. Burns glucose without oxygen. Produces lactate.
🫁
Oxidative System
Anything past 2 minutes. Uses oxygen to burn carbs and fat. Powers distance running and cycling.

The first two are anaerobic; the third is aerobic. The three systems never work in isolation — they overlap and hand off. A basketball player taps all three in a single possession: oxidative jogging up the court, glycolytic during a 30-second press, ATP-PC for the jump shot. The crossover between systems is what makes intermittent sports so demanding.

🧪Sport Science

Heart-rate variability (HRV) is the millisecond-level variation in time between heartbeats. A healthy, recovered nervous system shows high HRV — heartbeats are slightly irregular because the parasympathetic system is actively modulating each one. Chronic stress, illness, poor sleep, and overtraining all drop HRV measurably. Elite athletes now use morning HRV readings (a quick smartphone test) to decide whether to push a hard workout or take a recovery day. The science is sound: HRV trends predict overtraining better than perceived effort does.

3
Lesson 3
Heart-Rate Zones for Targeted Training

Your maximum heart rate can be roughly estimated as 220 minus your age, but the true equation is messier (and individual). For a 13-year-old, the estimate is about 207 BPM. Exercise physiologists divide all training intensities below max into five heart rate zones, each targeting a specific adaptation:

  • Zone 1 (50–60% of max) — Very easy. Recovery, warm-up.
  • Zone 2 (60–70%) — Conversational pace. Builds aerobic base. The "polarized training" zone elite endurance athletes spend ~80% of their volume in.
  • Zone 3 (70–80%) — Comfortably hard. Improves lactate clearance.
  • Zone 4 (80–90%) — Hard. Targets lactate threshold.
  • Zone 5 (90–100%) — All-out. Develops VO₂ max and neuromuscular power.

Most weekly cardio should sit in Zones 2 and 3. Short bursts in Zone 5 produce big adaptation but you can't sustain them — they should be used sparingly and with full recovery. The biggest mistake amateur runners make is too much time in Zone 3-4 ("medium hard") and not enough in either Zone 2 or Zone 5.

💡Did You Know?

Trained endurance athletes can have resting heart rates as low as 40 BPM — roughly half the rate of an average adult. The reason isn't weakness; it's the opposite. Each beat moves so much blood that the heart can fire less often to do the same delivery work. This number, called stroke volume, is one of the clearest signs of cardiovascular adaptation. Miguel Indurain, the five-time Tour de France winner, was famously measured with a resting heart rate of 28 BPM.

4
Try It
Six Cardio Modalities Compared
🏃
Steady Jog (Z2)
20–40 minutes. Builds aerobic base + capillary density.
🚴
Cycling
Low joint impact. Easy to control intensity by terrain and gearing.
⚡
HIIT Intervals
8 rounds of 30s hard / 60s easy. Targets glycolytic + VO₂ max efficiently.
🏊
Swimming
Full-body work with no joint impact. Excellent for recovery weeks.
🪜
Stair Climbing
Combines leg power with cardiac demand. Highly efficient per minute.
⚽
Sport Play
Recreational soccer, basketball, ultimate. Trains all three energy systems naturally.
📊Case Study

The Cooper Aerobics Center Longitudinal Study (40+ years, 80,000+ participants): Dr. Kenneth Cooper's team tested cardiovascular fitness in adults and tracked them for decades. The lowest-fitness group had roughly 3–4× the mortality rate of the highest-fitness group, even after controlling for diet, weight, blood pressure, and smoking. The effect was stronger than for any other measurable health variable. Lesson: cardiovascular fitness is not just about athletic performance. It's the most powerful longevity variable scientists have ever measured.

🌎Real-World Connection

Wearable HRV monitors (Whoop, Oura, Apple Watch) have moved this once-exclusive metric into everyday use. Elite teams have used it since the 2010s; college athletes now do too. But the technology is only as useful as the user's understanding. A 7-day rolling HRV trend tells you something. A single bad night does not. Pay attention to the patterns, not the daily noise — which is exactly how a real exercise physiologist reads any biological signal.

🔬Coach's Lab

4-week protocol: build your cardio baseline and watch it move. Week 1: Time yourself running a fixed distance (a half-mile or a single lap of a known course). Immediately take your heart rate (count for 15 seconds, multiply by 4). One minute later, take it again. Subtract — that's your 1-minute heart rate recovery. Record all three numbers (time, peak HR, 1-min recovery). Weeks 2–3: Run the same distance three times per week in Zone 2 (conversational pace — slower than the test). Week 4: Re-test at race effort. Faster time + lower peak HR + bigger 1-minute recovery = your cardiovascular system is adapting. If only one improves, the data tells you which sub-system responded fastest.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Cardiovascular fitness — Efficiency of heart, lungs, and vessels in delivering oxygen during exercise.
  • Aerobic — Activity that uses oxygen as the main energy source. Sustained, moderate intensity.
  • Anaerobic — Short, intense activity not relying on oxygen. Sprints, jumps, heavy lifts.
  • Heart rate zone — A percent-of-max range used to target specific physiological adaptations.
  • VO₂ max — Maximum volume of oxygen the body can use during all-out exercise (stretch term).
  • ATP-PC system — Energy pathway for efforts under 10 seconds (stretch term).
  • Glycolytic system — Energy pathway for 10s–2min efforts; produces lactate (stretch term).
  • HRV (heart rate variability) — Millisecond variation between heartbeats; high HRV indicates a recovered nervous system (stretch term).
📝Weekly Reflection

Critique prompt: A friend reads online that "HIIT is more efficient than steady cardio — 20 minutes of HIIT replaces an hour of jogging." Using the energy systems and heart-rate zones you read about, name two ways this claim is partially true AND two ways it's misleading. What kind of training is HIIT good at producing — and what kind does steady Zone 2 work do that HIIT can't replace?

pages.title: Week 9: Flexibility & Stretching
pages.html:
Optima
Academy Online
Mission: Move!
7th–8th Grade PE · Unit 1.5 · Flexibility and Stretching
Week 9

Flexibility and Stretching: The Range You Can Use

Flexibility sounds quieter than strength or speed, but every other physical skill is built on top of it. A pitcher with a stiff shoulder cannot throw fast. A sprinter with locked hips can't extend at full stride. A goalkeeper who can't drop into a split gives up the corner. This week we'll go beyond "stretch more" into a more useful framework: the difference between active and passive flexibility, why the body resists stretching, and the kind of protocols that actually change tissue over weeks — not just provide a temporary feel-good.

1
Lesson 1
What Flexibility Actually Is

Bones move because muscles pull on them. Each muscle crosses one or more joints, and that muscle's length determines how far the joint can travel. Short, tight muscle = limited range. Long, supple muscle = full range. Simple. But here's the catch: flexibility is not one number. It's joint-specific and even direction-specific. You can have flexible shoulders and tight hips. Flexible hip flexors and tight hamstrings. A good exercise physiologist tests each major joint separately, then targets the actual limiters.

There's also a difference between active flexibility (range you can reach using your own muscles) and passive flexibility (range you can reach with outside help — gravity, a partner, your own hands pulling). Passive range is almost always greater than active range. The gap matters: in a game, you only get to use the active version. Athletes who have lots of passive range but a big active-passive gap are at higher injury risk near end-of-range.

2
Lesson 2
Why the Body Resists Stretching

Inside every muscle are sensors called muscle spindles that monitor stretch and rate of stretch. When a muscle stretches quickly, the spindles fire a protective reflex called the stretch reflex — the muscle contracts to prevent damage. This is why fast, bouncy stretches don't work well, and why slow, sustained holds do. A 20–30 second hold gives the spindles time to relax and the muscle to actually lengthen.

But here's where it gets interesting. Most short-term flexibility gain isn't really tissue lengthening — it's stretch tolerance. Your nervous system gets used to the feel of end-range and stops firing the protective reflex as aggressively. Real tissue change takes much longer: 6–12 weeks of consistent training to measurably alter resting muscle length. Sport scientists call this the principle of specificity — your body adapts to the exact stress you apply, and only that stress, only if you apply it enough times.

🧪Sport Science

A 2014 meta-analysis of stretching studies (covering 125 trials) confirmed something coaches have known intuitively for years: stretching before a power or sprint activity reduces immediate performance by 2–5%. But the same studies also found that consistent stretching between sessions (3–5 days/week for 4+ weeks) measurably increases range of motion AND has modest injury-prevention effects in certain activities. The trick is timing: dynamic mobility before play, static stretching after or in standalone sessions.

3
Lesson 3
What Actually Works: Dose and Method

Three methods of flexibility training, in order of evidence strength:

  • Static stretching — holding a position 20–60 seconds. The most studied; best for long-term range gains. Do after activity or in separate sessions.
  • Dynamic stretching — moving through full range repeatedly. Best before activity. Does not produce long-term range gains by itself.
  • PNF (proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation) — alternating 6–10 second muscle contractions with 20–30 second stretches. Most effective method for fast range gains. Usually done with a partner.

Required dose for visible change: 3–5 sessions per week, 4+ weeks minimum. One session changes nothing. A habit changes everything.

4
Try It
Six Foundation Stretches
🦋
Butterfly
Sit, soles together. Gently press knees toward floor. Adductors. 45s.
🦩
Standing Quad
Pull heel to glute. 30s per side.
🤲
Standing Toe Touch
Slow reach to toes. Hamstrings + lower back. 30s.
🐶
Downward Dog
Hands and feet on floor, hips up. Calves, hamstrings, shoulders. 30s.
🐍
Cobra
Face down, press chest up. Opens hip flexors and front of body. 30s.
🧘
Pigeon Pose
Front shin across body, back leg extended. Deep glute + hip rotator. 60s per side.
💡Did You Know?

Gymnasts and ballet dancers don't have naturally elastic tissue — most start training before age 6 and stretch 1–2 hours every single day for years. That's the actual dose required to reach a full split or a backbend. The takeaway is honest: flexibility is earned through consistent reps, not gifted at birth. But measurable change is possible at any age with much smaller doses — even 10 minutes a day, 4 days per week, produces real ROM gains in 4 weeks.

📊Case Study

Simone Biles and the body-awareness science: When Biles withdrew from the 2021 Olympic team gymnastics final, she described "the twisties" — a sudden loss of mid-air spatial awareness. Sport psychologists call this a proprioceptive disruption: the body's sensors stop accurately reporting where you are in space. The condition is real, dangerous in gymnastics, and connected to mental fatigue, stress, and overtraining. Lesson: flexibility, body control, and mental state are tightly coupled. Elite athletes train all three together — and rest when any one of them fails.

🌎Real-World Connection

NFL kickers spend 20+ minutes before every game opening hip flexors — if the hip can't fully extend, the kick loses measurable power. NBA centers spend hours weekly on ankle and hip mobility so they can land safely from jumps. The U.S. Olympic Training Center tests passive and active flexibility on every incoming athlete because the actual performance limiter is often a tight joint, not a weak muscle. Athletic trainers, physical therapists, and exercise physiologists all build careers around solving range-of-motion problems.

🔬Coach's Lab

6-week ROM protocol with re-testing. Test your seated toe-touch: sit with legs straight, reach forward, measure how far past your toes you can reach (inches past = positive; inches short = negative). Record. Now run a 3×/week static stretching protocol for 6 weeks: hamstring stretch (3 × 30s) + butterfly (3 × 45s) + downward dog (3 × 30s). At Weeks 3 and 6, re-test the toe touch. A 2–4 inch gain in 6 weeks is realistic. If your number didn't move, examine the variables: did you actually do 3 sessions per week? Did you hold long enough? Did you stretch the right muscles for the test? An exercise physiologist diagnoses missed gains by interrogating the variables — not by guessing.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Flexibility — A muscle or joint's ability to move through its full range of motion.
  • Range of motion (ROM) — How far a joint can move comfortably under control.
  • Active flexibility — Range reachable using only your own muscles.
  • Passive flexibility — Range reachable with outside help (gravity, a partner).
  • Specificity — Training adapts to the exact stress applied — and only that stress (stretch term).
  • Muscle spindle — Sensor inside a muscle; triggers protective contraction during fast stretch (stretch term).
  • PNF — Proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation; alternating contractions and stretches (stretch term).
  • Proprioception — Body's awareness of its own position in space (stretch term).
📝Weekly Reflection

Critique prompt: A coach tells the team that "stretching prevents injury." Looking at what you read about stretching research, name two ways this statement is supported by evidence AND two ways it's misleading or incomplete. What kind of injuries does stretching actually help with, and what kind doesn't it help with at all?

→What's Next

pages.title: Week 11: Nutrition
pages.html:
Optima
Academy Online
Mission: Move!
7th–8th Grade PE · Unit 1.6 · Nutrition
Week 11

Nutrition: Engineering Fuel and Recovery

An exercise physiologist treats food the same way they treat training — as a controlled input that creates measurable output. The carbs you eat become muscle glycogen. The protein becomes new fiber. The hydration becomes the blood volume that delivers oxygen. None of it is magic, and none of it is optional. This week we'll cover macronutrients, micronutrients, hydration, and two concepts that show up in every serious sports-nutrition conversation: the protein synthesis window and glycogen depletion/replenishment.

1
Lesson 1
The Three Macronutrients

Nearly every food contains some mix of three macronutrients — large-volume nutrients the body needs in significant amounts. Each one has a specific job:

🍞
Carbohydrates
Body's preferred fuel. Stored as glycogen in muscles and liver. Grains, fruits, vegetables, dairy.
🍗
Proteins
Building blocks for muscle, bone, skin, blood. Meat, eggs, beans, dairy, nuts.
🥑
Fats
Long-lasting energy + brain and hormone support. Oils, nuts, avocado, fish.

You need all three. Cutting any one out leaves a system short on something it needs. Researchers who study eating disorders in young athletes flag chronic restriction of fat or carbs as one of the most damaging patterns in youth sport — it shows up as recurrent injuries, fatigue, mood disruption, and slower recovery.

2
Lesson 2
Micronutrients, Hydration, and Electrolytes

Beyond macros, your body needs small doses of micronutrients — vitamins and minerals — to keep the system running. The most performance-relevant for adolescent athletes:

  • Iron — helps blood carry oxygen. Low iron measurably reduces endurance. (Red meat, beans, spinach.)
  • Calcium + Vitamin D — bone-building partners. Especially critical during adolescent growth years.
  • B Vitamins — convert food to usable energy. (Whole grains, leafy greens, eggs.)
  • Sodium, Potassium, Magnesium — electrolytes that conduct the electrical signals running every muscle contraction.

The body is about 60% water by mass. Even mild dehydration (a 2% loss of body water) measurably reduces strength, endurance, and concentration. During hard sweat you lose both water and electrolytes — which is why long endurance events use sports drinks rather than plain water, while shorter sessions usually need only water.

🧪Sport Science

When you eat carbs, your body breaks them into glucose. Glucose either gets used immediately as fuel or gets stored in muscle and liver as glycogen. During hard exercise, muscles tap that glycogen reserve — usually enough for about 90–120 minutes of moderate-to-hard work before depletion. The famous marathon "bonk" or "hitting the wall" is glycogen depletion in action. Distance athletes "carb-load" before key events to top up glycogen tanks, and they refuel mid-race because they can't store enough to finish.

3
Lesson 3
Eat the Rainbow + the Microbiome

Different colored fruits and vegetables contain different vitamins, minerals, and plant compounds called phytonutrients. The more colors on your plate over time, the broader your nutrient profile and the stronger most measurable health markers tend to be.

🍎
Red
Tomatoes, strawberries, peppers. Lycopene, heart health.
🥕
Orange/Yellow
Carrots, sweet potatoes. Beta-carotene, immune and eye support.
🥦
Green
Broccoli, spinach, kale. Folate, iron, calcium, magnesium.
🫐
Blue/Purple
Blueberries, eggplant. Anthocyanins, anti-inflammatory.
🧄
White
Garlic, onions, cauliflower. Sulfur compounds, immune support.
💡Did You Know?

Your gut contains trillions of bacteria — the microbiome — that help digest food and even communicate with your brain through what researchers call the gut-brain axis. The single strongest evidence-backed way to build a healthy, diverse microbiome is to eat a wide variety of plants. One large study found that people who ate 30+ different plant foods per week had significantly more diverse gut bacteria than people who ate fewer than 10. Lesson: variety matters as much as quantity.

4
Lesson 4
The Performance Plate and Protein Timing

The simplest applied tool is the MyPlate model: ½ fruits and vegetables, ¼ grains (preferably whole), ¼ protein, with a side of dairy or calcium alternative. For athletes there's a useful nuance called the protein synthesis window. The 1–2 hours after training is when your body is most primed to rebuild muscle from food. Consuming 15–25 grams of protein in that window measurably amplifies the muscle-repair response. That's a glass of milk, a yogurt cup, a slice of turkey on bread, or a small chicken breast.

The glycogen replenishment window runs in parallel: the first 30–60 minutes post-exercise is the best time to refill muscle glycogen with carbohydrates. For most middle-school athletes a normal post-practice meal handles both jobs at once.

📊Case Study

The 2021 Tokyo Olympics nutrition data: The U.S. Olympic Committee employs full-time sports dietitians who track macronutrient intake for elite athletes. Their data showed that swimmers competing in multiple events were averaging 5,000–8,000 calories per day — sometimes more than gymnasts and divers combined. Why? Energy demand. A 2-hour pool session can burn 2,000+ calories. Lesson: there's no universal "right amount to eat." It depends on the actual energy expenditure of your activity — which is exactly the kind of variable an exercise physiologist measures.

🌎Real-World Connection

Professional teams employ sports dietitians who plan meals down to the gram. An NBA player might consume 4,000 calories a day during the season, carefully timed around practices. An Olympic gymnast might eat 2,000 calories with extra protein and calcium for bone health. The principle stays the same regardless of sport: match input to the system you're training. Career paths in this field — registered dietitian (RD), certified sports nutritionist (CSSD), food scientist — are growing fast.

🔬Coach's Lab

2-week protocol: track and optimize your post-workout fuel. Week 1 (observation): After every workout, write down what you ate within 60 minutes (or note "nothing"). Track your perceived energy and soreness the next day on a 1–10 scale. Week 2 (intervention): After every workout, eat 15–25 grams of protein within the synthesis window (Greek yogurt + fruit, peanut butter on toast, a turkey wrap, a glass of milk). Continue the perceived-energy tracking. Compare Week 1 vs Week 2. Did your next-day soreness change? Did your energy change? If the difference is large, you've measured a real effect on your own body. If it's small, the variable you changed wasn't your limiter.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Macronutrients — The three large-volume nutrients: carbs, protein, fat.
  • Micronutrients — Vitamins and minerals — small amounts, essential function.
  • Carbohydrates — Body's preferred fuel; stored as glycogen.
  • Protein — Used to build and repair tissue.
  • Glycogen — Stored carbohydrate in muscles and liver (stretch term).
  • Electrolytes — Minerals (sodium, potassium, magnesium) that conduct electrical signals in nerves and muscles (stretch term).
  • Protein synthesis window — The 1–2 hours after training when the body is most primed to rebuild muscle (stretch term).
  • Glycogen replenishment window — The 30–60 minutes post-exercise when muscle glycogen refills fastest (stretch term).
📝Weekly Reflection

Critique prompt: An influencer claims that "you need to eat protein every 3 hours or you'll lose muscle." Using what you read about the protein synthesis window and overall daily protein needs, name two reasons this claim is partially supported AND two reasons it's overstated. What's actually true about protein timing for a middle-school athlete?

→What's Next

pages.html:
Optima

7th–8th Grade PE · Unit 1.7 · Locomotor Skills
Week 13

Locomotor Skills: The Movement Alphabet

Every athletic skill is built from locomotion — moving the body through space. Biomechanists count eight foundational locomotor patterns; together they're the alphabet of athletic movement. A sprinter, a goalkeeper, a dancer, and a basketball point guard all combine these eight patterns into something more complex. The principle of specificity matters: your body adapts to the exact patterns you practice. Train all eight and your movement vocabulary grows; train only one and your gaps stay gaps.

1
Lesson 1
The Eight Locomotor Skills
🚶
Walking
One foot always on the ground. Heel-strike, midstance, push-off — the most efficient gait at slow speeds.
🏃
Running
Both feet leave the ground between steps. Includes a true flight phase — and 2–3× body-weight impact.
🦘
Hopping
Push off and land on the same foot. Tests single-leg power and unilateral balance.
🤾
Jumping
Push off two feet, land on two feet. Bilateral power output.
🐴
Galloping
One foot leads, the other catches up. Same lead foot stays in front — asymmetric gait.
⏭️
Skipping
Step + hop, alternating sides. Tests rhythm and cross-body coordination.
↔️
Sliding
Lateral movement — one foot leads, the other catches up. Critical for defenders.
🦌
Leaping
Push off one foot, land on the other. Asymmetric power transfer.
🧪Sport Science

The brain region that controls these patterns is the motor cortex, with deep involvement from the cerebellum (coordination) and basal ganglia (movement initiation). Every rep strengthens neural pathways through a process called myelination — the insulation around neurons gets thicker and signals travel faster. After enough reps the pattern becomes automatic; sport scientists call this motor learning consolidation. It is not stored in muscles — it's stored in the brain as a faster, smoother neural circuit.

2
Lesson 2
Stride Mechanics: Frequency vs. Length

Sprinting speed is the product of just two variables: stride frequency (how many steps per second) × stride length (how far you travel per step). Top sprinters score high on both — Usain Bolt averages roughly 4.5 strides per second at 2.5 meters each. But the two variables interact in interesting ways. Increase stride length past your optimum and frequency drops; force higher frequency and length shortens. Elite coaches optimize the product, not the individual numbers.

The two variables also have different limiters. Frequency is mostly limited by the nervous system — how fast you can fire and reset muscles. Length is mostly limited by hip mobility and force production (how hard you push the ground). Knowing which one is your bottleneck tells you what to train.

3
Lesson 3
Biomechanics: Ground Reaction Force and Lever Classes

Every time your foot pushes down, the ground pushes back with equal force — ground reaction force (GRF). At sprint speed, your foot strikes with 3–5 times your body weight, and the ground returns that force into your stride. Technique determines how much you get back. A sprinter who lands cleanly on the ball of the foot uses GRF efficiently. A heel-striker loses energy to the ground absorbing the impact.

Bones act as levers that muscles pull on to create motion. There are three lever classes:

  • 1st class — fulcrum between effort and load. Example: tilting the head (atlas joint as fulcrum).
  • 2nd class — load between fulcrum and effort. Example: standing on tiptoes (ball of foot as fulcrum, body weight as load, calf as effort).
  • 3rd class — effort between fulcrum and load. Example: bicep curl (elbow as fulcrum, hand/weight as load, bicep as effort). Most body movements are 3rd-class — they sacrifice mechanical advantage for speed.
💡Did You Know?

Astronauts returning from the International Space Station have to re-learn walking. After six months in microgravity, the brain's motor program for ground reaction force gets overwritten — their legs literally don't know how hard to push. NASA puts returning astronauts through structured locomotor rehab (the same eight patterns you're working on) to rebuild the motor program. Recovery takes 1–3 months of daily practice. Even "automatic" skills are maintained by use — and rebuilt the same way they were first built.

4
Try It
Locomotor Skill Circuit

Run this 4-minute circuit: 30 seconds on each pattern, no rest between. Focus on quality and reading your own mechanics, not just speed.

  1. Walk forward with deliberate heel-to-toe contact
  2. Jog at conversational pace, observing your foot strike
  3. Hop on right foot 15 seconds, switch to left for 15
  4. Jump in place with soft, controlled landings — knees over toes
  5. Gallop forward, then switch lead leg halfway through
  6. Skip with high knees and tall posture — focus on rhythm
  7. Slide sideways — left direction, then right
  8. Leap forward over a chalk line, focus on soft single-leg landing
📊Case Study

Usain Bolt's 9.58s 100m world record (Berlin, 2009): Biomechanists who broke down the race frame-by-frame found Bolt's secret wasn't fastest top speed — it was the longest sustained top speed of any sprinter ever measured. He hit ~44 km/h around the 60m mark and held it through 80m, when nearly every competitor decelerates. Stride length: ~2.45 meters. Stride frequency: ~4.4 per second. Lesson: elite performance isn't always about a single dominant variable. Sometimes it's about maintaining excellent values for longer than anyone else can.

🌎Real-World Connection

Olympic-level track coaches still use locomotor drills with elite sprinters. "A-skips" and "B-skips," high-knee runs, and side shuffles appear in nearly every world-class warm-up. The basics don't stop being useful — coaches just extract more force and less waste from them. Career paths include biomechanist, sports performance coach, kinesiologist, and physical therapist — all of them growing fields that use motion-capture, force-plate, and pressure-sensor technology to make movement measurable.

🔬Coach's Lab

4-week protocol: improve your vertical jump. Week 1: Mark your standing reach (highest point you can touch flat-footed). Then do a max vertical jump and mark the top in chalk. Subtract — that's your baseline vertical leap. Weeks 2–3: Run a 3×/week jump training program: 3 sets of 5 squat jumps + 3 sets of 8 broad jumps + 3 sets of 10 single-leg hops per leg. Week 4: Re-test the vertical jump. A 2–5 inch improvement in 4 weeks is realistic at your age. If your number didn't move, examine variables: was your jump-test technique the same? Did you actually train 3 sessions per week? Were you well-rested for the re-test? Diagnose by data, not by feel.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Locomotion — Moving the body from one place to another.
  • Locomotor skills — The 8 fundamental movement patterns: walk, run, hop, jump, gallop, skip, slide, leap.
  • Stride frequency — Steps per second — limited mostly by nervous system speed.
  • Stride length — Distance traveled per step — limited mostly by mobility and force production.
  • Motor cortex — Brain region controlling voluntary movement (stretch term).
  • Ground reaction force (GRF) — The push-back the ground gives your foot when it strikes (stretch term).
  • Lever class — Categorization (1st/2nd/3rd) of how muscles, bones, and loads arrange around a joint (stretch term).
  • Motor learning consolidation — The process by which practiced movements get stored as faster neural circuits (stretch term).
📝Weekly Reflection

Multi-variable design prompt: Two sprinters both run 100m in 13.5 seconds. Sprinter A has a stride frequency of 4.1/sec and stride length of 1.8m. Sprinter B has frequency 3.7/sec and length 2.0m. Both have plateaued for a month. Design a different training plan for each — what specifically would you have each one train, and why? Then identify one measurement you'd use to verify the plan worked.

→What's Next

pages.title: Week 15: Throwing and Catching
pages.html:
Optima
Academy Online
Mission: Move!
7th–8th Grade PE · Unit 1.8 · Manipulative Skills: Throwing and Catching
Week 15

Throwing and Catching: The Kinetic Chain

Throwing and catching are manipulative skills — movements that control an object rather than just the body. They look simple, but a powerful throw uses every major body segment firing in a precise sequence: legs, hips, core, shoulder, elbow, wrist, fingers. This is called the kinetic chain, and it shows up in baseball, football, javelin, even shot put. Get the order right and the ball flies fast and on line. Get it wrong and you lose 50% of available power.

1
Lesson 1
The Mechanics of an Overhand Throw

A powerful overhand throw transfers energy from the ground up. Each body segment adds speed to the next, like cracking a whip. The seven steps:

  1. Stand sideways — the non-throwing shoulder points at the target
  2. Step toward the target with the opposite foot (right hand throws → left foot steps)
  3. Rotate the hips as the foot lands and weight transfers forward
  4. Drive the throwing shoulder forward as hip rotation completes
  5. Whip the arm through — elbow leads, hand follows
  6. Snap the wrist on release for spin and accuracy
  7. Follow through — the hand finishes near the opposite hip

Energy moves from large, slow segments (legs, hips) to small, fast ones (wrist, fingers). The hips reach roughly 700°/sec rotational velocity; the wrist hits up to 7,000°/sec at release. Skip any step and the chain collapses.

🧪Sport Science

Major League Baseball pitchers generate roughly 50% of their throwing velocity from their legs and hips alone. The arm is the final link that releases the accumulated energy. This is why elite pitchers spend much of their offseason in the weight room building lower-body strength. Studies on UCL (ulnar collateral ligament) injuries show that pitchers with weak hip and core musculature are 2–3× more likely to need "Tommy John" elbow surgery — the chain breaks where the weakest link is, and a weak base puts all the stress on the arm.

2
Lesson 2
Catching: Tracking, Positioning, Receiving

Catching looks like one skill but is actually three working together:

  • Tracking — keeping eyes on the ball from release to arrival
  • Positioning — moving feet so the ball arrives in front of the chest
  • Receiving — soft hands that give a little on impact so the ball doesn't bounce out

For most middle-school athletes, positioning is the bottleneck. You have to move your feet, not just reach with your arms. Watch a great outfielder: they're moving the instant the bat makes contact, and by the time the ball arrives they're already underneath it. Great catchers are great foot-movers first.

3
Lesson 3
Throws for Different Situations
🎯
Overhand
Long distance, maximum power. Baseball outfield, football, javelin.
🥎
Underhand Toss
Short distance, gentle arc. Softball pitch, beanbag toss, basketball pass.
🏀
Two-Handed Pass
Fast and accurate. Basketball chest pass, soccer throw-in.
⚾
Sidearm
Lower release angle, faster release. Quick infield throws, skipping a stone.
💡Did You Know?

Humans are the only animals that throw with both speed and accuracy. Chimpanzees throw, but only at about 20 mph and rarely on target. Anthropologists found that the human shoulder evolved a uniquely flexible structure roughly 2 million years ago — the storage of elastic energy in the shoulder ligaments lets us "wind up" and release at speeds no other primate can match. Researchers think this throwing ability gave early humans a major survival advantage, both for hunting (a thrown rock from 30 meters away beats face-to-face combat) and for defense.

4
Try It
Throw and Catch Drills
🧱
Wall Throw
Throw against a wall, catch the rebound. 20 reps each hand.
🪣
Bucket Toss
Underhand toss into a bucket from 5 feet. Move it back as accuracy improves.
👥
Partner Catch
Throw and catch from 10 feet. Step into every throw — practice the chain.
👆
Self-Toss + Clap
Toss the ball up, clap once, catch with both hands. Add a clap each round.
📊Case Study

Aroldis Chapman's 105.1 mph fastball (2010 MLB record): Biomechanists at the American Sports Medicine Institute analyzed Chapman's mechanics on high-speed cameras. They found his shoulder rotated at 9,400°/sec — the fastest joint rotation ever measured in any human movement. The catch: that velocity produces forces on his elbow ligaments roughly equal to his entire body weight. Pitching at the elite level is a high-reward, high-risk profession. Lesson: maximum performance often pushes biological tissues right up to their structural limits — which is why injury prevention and recovery are core to any throwing program.

🌎Real-World Connection

NFL quarterbacks throw a football about 60 mph with pinpoint accuracy at moving targets while being chased by 300-pound defenders. The exact same kinetic chain you're learning — sideways stance, step, hip rotation, follow-through — is what a Super Bowl winner uses. The pros have just done it tens of millions more times. Pitching coaches and biomechanists now use motion-capture (the same tech used in video games) to break down each pitcher's mechanics frame by frame and find subtle inefficiencies.

🔬Coach's Lab

3-week protocol: diagnose and fix your throwing kinetic chain. Week 1: Throw a tennis ball at a wall, hard but with control. Have a partner record slow-motion video. Watch and score yourself 0–3 on three checkpoints: (1) opposite foot stepping toward target, (2) hips rotating before arm comes forward, (3) hand finishing near opposite hip. Whatever scored lowest is your priority. Weeks 2–3: Drill only the weakest link 3×/week (10 minutes per session, 50 focused reps). End of Week 3: Re-record video. Did the broken link improve? Did your throw also feel/look harder? That's how a biomechanist diagnoses and treats a chain breakdown.

5

Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know

  • Overhand throw — Arm comes over the shoulder — used for distance and power.
  • Underhand toss — Arm swings below the shoulder — short, soft passes.
  • Kinetic chain — Sequence of body segments transferring force from ground to ball (stretch term).
  • Follow-through — Continuing the motion after release — adds power and accuracy.
  • Soft hands — Hands that give on impact so the ball doesn't bounce out.
  • Center of mass — The balance point of the body during movement (stretch term).
  • Elastic energy storage — Tendons and ligaments storing energy during a wind-up that's released at the throw (stretch term).

🚀 Flight Club Challenge

After learning about nutrition, fuel up and try these three moves. Flamingo Balance trains stability, Butterfly opens your hips, and Arm Circles wake up your shoulders.

1
Flamingo Balance
  1. Stand up tall with your feet together.
  2. Gently lift one foot and bend your knee so your foot is behind you.
  3. Hold your arms out to the side like wings for balance.
  4. Try to stay still like a flamingo for 10 seconds.
  5. Switch legs and repeat.

Optional: Try closing one eye or flapping your "wings" for a fun challenge!

Benefits: Builds focus and body control, helping you stay calm and centered.

2
Butterfly Stretch

How to Do It:

  • Sit on the floor with feet together and knees bent outward.
  • Hold your feet with your hands and gently push your knees toward the floor.
  • Keep your back straight and hold the stretch.
  • Optional: Pretend your legs are butterfly wings and gently flap them!

Benefits: Stretches the inner thighs and hips.

3
Arm Circles
  1. Stand up straight with your arms stretched out to the sides, like a big "T."
  2. Slowly make small forward circles with your arms for 10 seconds.
  3. Then, switch directions and make small backward circles for 10 seconds.
  4. Want a challenge? Try making the circles bigger each time!

Optional: Pretend you're flying like a superhero or spinning like a windmill!

Benefits: Warms up your shoulder and arm muscles to get ready for movement.

Week 14
🚀 Flight Club Challenge

Three strength moves that hit your legs, core, and arms. Locomotor skills depend on these muscle groups — this challenge builds the engine.

1
Split Squat
  1. Stand up tall with one foot in front and the other foot behind you — like you're about to take a big step.
  2. Keep your front knee over your ankle and your back heel lifted off the ground.
  3. Slowly bend both knees to lower your body straight down.
  4. Stop when your back knee is close to the ground (but not touching!).
  5. Stand back up. Do 5 slow squats, then switch legs and repeat.

Benefits: Makes your leg muscles stronger, especially your thighs and calves.

2
Superman Hold
  1. Lie flat on your stomach on the floor or a soft mat.
  2. Stretch your arms straight out in front of you and your legs straight behind you.
  3. At the same time, lift your arms, chest, and legs slightly off the ground.
  4. Try to hold this pose for 10 seconds — like you're flying through the sky!
  5. Slowly lower back down and rest. Try it again 2–3 more times!

Benefits: Strengthens your back and core muscles.

3
Bench Dips
  1. Find a sturdy chair, bench, or low table. Sit on the edge with your hands next to your hips.
  2. Walk your feet forward and slide your bottom off the edge, so your hands are holding you up.
  3. Bend your elbows to lower your body a little — like you're going down slowly.
  4. Push back up until your arms are straight again.
  5. Try doing 5–10 dips, then take a break!

Benefits: Strengthens your arms, shoulders, and chest.

🏃Activity Cue

Submit a video demonstrating the challenges. The more you do, the more points you get in Flight Club!

quizzes.title: Quiz 1: Why We Move + Warm-Ups & Cool-Downs

questions.text: Marcus has 10 minutes before kickoff. Choose the BEST way for him to spend that time as a sport scientist would advise.

answers.text: Sit on the bench so his muscles stay rested and fresh for the game.
5 minutes of light jogging followed by 5 minutes of dynamic stretches like leg swings and arm circles.
10 minutes of long static stretches (each held for 60 seconds) — flexibility is always good before a game.
Eat a large meal so he has fuel for the next 90 minutes.

questions.text: Why does a proper warm-up measurably IMPROVE performance — not just reduce injury risk?

answers.text: It tricks the brain into thinking exercise is already over so muscles relax.
It cools muscles so they save energy until they are needed.
It raises core body temperature, increases blood flow to muscles, and lubricates joints so muscles produce force faster.
It burns enough calories to give you extra fuel during the workout.

questions.text: Which body system has the primary job of delivering oxygen to working muscles?

answers.text: The skeletal system.
The cardiovascular system.
The nervous system.
The digestive system.

Gradually increasing training demand (reps, sets, or load) over time so the body keeps adapting.
Lifting the heaviest possible weight on the first day to shock the muscles.
